articles.title: Corporate Profits Surge Amid Concerns Over Sustainability
articles.summary: A closer look at earnings as a percentage of GDP reveals a concerning trend, with corporate profitability being unsustainable in the long term.
articles.content: The stock market's recent surge has left investors wondering if corporate profits can continue to drive growth. However, a closer look at earnings as a percentage of GDP reveals a concerning trend. Historically, high levels of profitability have been short-lived, and experts warn that the current situation may be unsustainable. According to Sahil Kapoor, executive director of DSP mutual fund in Mumbai, "Historically, these levels of profitability don't last long." He notes that corporate profitability is the most mean-reverting series in finance. This means that high profits tend to revert back to average levels over time. A chart of earnings as a percentage of national income shows just how far we've deviated from past trends. For decades, this ratio hovered between 6% and 7%. However, it shot up to 10% during the dot.com bubble, plummeted during the GFC in 2008-2009, and remained steady at around 11% until recently. The current surge in profitability is largely driven by sectors such as software, memory providers, and energy producers. The government's latest figures show that earnings as a percentage of GDP reached 13.37% in the third quarter. This is an increase from 13.14% in Q2 and marks a significant departure from past trends. While corporate profits have been soaring, experts warn that this trend may not be sustainable. The ratio of earnings to national income has never been as high as it is today. This raises concerns about the potential for a correction or even a recession. The implications of these high profit levels are far-reaching and could impact the stock market in significant ways. As investors, it's essential to consider the long-term outlook and not get caught up in short-term fluctuations. Corporate profits are surging at a pace that's leaving many market strategists bewildered. The latest data shows nominal GDP grew 6% in the year ending Q3 2026, but corporate earnings jumped a whopping 23%, from $3.59 trillion to $4.42 trillion. This unprecedented divergence has led Wall Street to predict another 25% increase in profits by the end of 2027. If that happens, the ratio of earnings to GDP would soar to an astonishing 15.7%, more than twice the average over the past eight decades and a staggering 40% above the level two decades ago. However, history suggests that such exceptional profitability is short-lived. Two primary forces are poised to push profits back down to earth: rising wages and shareholder demands for a bigger share of the revenue pie. As workers increasingly voice their discontent, unions will likely step up pressure on corporations to distribute more of the bounty among employees. The consequences of this trend can be seen in recent elections, where voters have begun to rebel against economic systems that favor the wealthy at the expense of the working class. According to Rob Arnott, founder and chairman of Syzygy Asset Management, "I have often observed that when profits rise relative to wages, voters can rebel." The widening gap between corporate profits and worker compensation is a ticking time bomb. As capital continues to reap an ever-larger share of revenues, workers will demand a fairer slice of the economic pie. This growing divide has significant implications for investors, who must consider the long-term outlook rather than getting caught up in short-term fluctuations. The semiconductor market is witnessing a high-stakes game of cat and mouse as companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet rush to develop their own cheaper versions of expensive chips from Nvidia. This aggressive move is likely aimed at reducing costs and increasing profit margins in an industry where competition is fierce. Economists point out that the shift in profits towards GDP may be more than just a temporary phenomenon. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, suggests that the ratio has permanently reset to higher levels due to several factors. One key reason is the decline of worker bargaining power as union membership dwindles. The benefits of recent productivity increases are flowing disproportionately to businesses rather than workers, according to Zandi. He notes that this trend is exacerbated by the rise of "superstar companies that dominate their industries and gain an advantage from Trump's tariffs, which restrict foreign competition. The surge in corporate profits has left many economists concerned that it's unsustainable and may eventually lead to a sharp decline. Zandi points out that some of the factors contributing to this spike are unlikely to be repeated, particularly the tax cuts which could be reversed at any time. A significant increase in prices is also seen as unlikely to recur, leaving Wall Street's optimism about future profits growth as its main concern according to Zandi. Many money managers believe that corporate profits will continue to outpace economic growth indefinitely, a view that has some experts warning of an impending market correction. This kind of thinking often precedes significant market downturns and a sharp sell-off is seen as increasingly likely by those who expect the current trend to be reversed. The rapid rise in corporate profits from 11% to its current level of 13.4% has made them particularly vulnerable to a decline, or at least a prolonged period of stagnation. The surge in corporate profits has reached a critical juncture, prompting concerns about their sustainability. According to economic theory, such a spike is unlikely to last indefinitely. Profits exceeding 13.4% of GDP have historically been followed by a decline or prolonged stagnation, and this trend may be repeating itself. Friedman's warning that profits cannot rise beyond a certain share of GDP for long" seems increasingly relevant in the face of current market dynamics.
